name: Voice surgery (cricothyroid approximation)

angle.text: Cricothyroid approximation raises pitch by tensioning the vocal folds and has mainly been used for voice feminisation. The pitch change is measurable after surgery; newer techniques have largely replaced it.

summary: Surgery that tightens the vocal folds to raise pitch; largely superseded and can leave a falsetto voice.
note: Irreversible surgery; outcomes may decline over time.
currentQuick:
CTA moves two laryngeal cartilages together to tension the vocal folds and raise pitch, mainly for voice feminisation.
Reviews report mixed results for older techniques, and fewer surgeons offer it now.
How it works: Bringing the cricoid and thyroid cartilages closer lengthens and tenses the folds, raising pitch.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include falsetto-locked voice, loss of loudness or quality, swallowing or breathing problems, infection and scarring; effects may decline over time.
deepLead:
Cricothyroid approximation (CTA) is a voice surgery that raises pitch by moving the cricoid and thyroid cartilages closer together, tensioning and lengthening the vocal folds. It has mainly been used for voice feminisation in transgender women.
Wikipedia reports that CTA often leaves patients locked into falsetto, that outcomes may decline over time, and that fewer clinicians perform it now than Wendler glottoplasty. A 2017 systematic review of pitch-raising surgery in male-to-female transsexual patients found mixed results, while a 2025 meta-analysis reported that surgery generally produced larger and more lasting pitch gains than voice therapy.

name: Adam's apple enhancement

angle.text: Surgical enlargement of the Adam's apple adds a visible neck prominence, described mainly as part of facial masculinization for transmasculine patients. The change is directly visible; evidence is a handful of small case series.

summary: Surgical enlargement of the Adam's apple, documented mostly in transmasculine facial masculinization; evidence is a handful of small case series.
note: Surgery near the larynx; only small case series published.
currentQuick:
Adam's apple enhancement enlarges the bump at the front of the neck, usually with a custom implant or cartilage work, to give a more masculine neckline.
It appears in the literature chiefly as part of facial masculinization surgery for transmasculine patients. Published data are small series.
How it works: A surgeon adds volume over the thyroid cartilage, in the reported case series using a patient-specific PEEK implant designed from scans.
Risks and caveats: As with any surgery near the larynx, complications are possible; the reported series is only six patients, so rates are not established.
deepLead:
Adam's apple enhancement, sometimes called laryngeal or tracheal augmentation, is a surgical procedure that enlarges the visible laryngeal prominence at the front of the neck, which is typically more pronounced in men.  It is described in the medical literature mainly as one component of facial masculinization surgery for transmasculine patients, alongside mandible angle and chin procedures. 
Published evidence is limited to small surgical series; one 2025 report followed six transmasculine patients who received personalized PEEK implants planned with virtual surgical planning.  Within looksmaxxing communities the topic appears as a hardmaxxing option for a more masculine neck, though no community-specific studies were found.

name: Neck training for voice

angle.text: Looksmaxxing communities propose that strengthening and thickening the neck deepens the voice, alongside a thicker-looking neck. No published studies test the voice claim.

summary: The idea that thicker neck muscles lower your voice; no studies have tested it.
currentQuick:
Some people say training the neck makes the voice deeper.
No studies were found testing this.
How it works: Proponents' reasoning is that a thicker neck changes resonance; standard sources attribute pitch mainly to vocal fold size and laryngeal growth. [1]
Risks and caveats: No specific risks were documented for this claim; heavy neck exercise carries general injury risks.
deepLead: Neck training for voice refers to the belief, circulating in looksmaxxing communities, that strengthening or thickening neck muscles can deepen the voice. No published studies examining this claim were found.

name: Hydration and humidifier for voice

angle.text: Users drink water and humidify rooms to keep vocal folds moist for a clearer, smoother voice. Hydration has been examined with vocal rest in relation to vocal fatigue in karaoke singers; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: Drinking water and humidifying the room to keep vocal folds moist; studied only loosely, and humidifiers need upkeep.
note: Dirty or overused humidifiers can cause problems.
currentQuick:
Hydration and humidifiers are used to keep the voice comfortable and less fatigued.
One small study of karaoke singers tested hydration with rest; little else is specific to this use.
How it works: Proponents say moisture lubricates the vocal folds; humidifiers add moisture to air.
Risks and caveats: Humidifiers can spread microorganisms if unclean and promote mold when humidity is too high. [2]
deepLead:
Hydration and humidifier use for the voice is a set of practices, drinking water and humidifying room air, that people adopt in the belief that moist vocal folds work better and recover faster. A study of karaoke singers examined hydration together with vocal rest in relation to vocal fatigue.
Humidifiers are described generally as helping with dry mucous membranes and cough, but also carry contamination and overuse risks.

name: Throat coat tea

angle.text: Singers and voice-conscious users drink slippery-elm herbal teas such as Throat Coat for throat comfort and a smoother voice. Use is traditional; no clinical studies of these teas were found.

summary: Slippery-elm-style herbal teas for a soothed throat; traditional use, no trials.
currentQuick:
Throat teas are drunk for comfort before or after heavy voice use.
They rest on traditional use rather than trial data.
How it works: Slippery elm is described as a demulcent, a coating soothing agent. [1]
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed did not describe adverse effects.
deepLead: Throat Coat tea refers to herbal teas sold for throat comfort, commonly built around slippery elm, a plant whose inner bark has long been used in folk medicine for sore throat and sold in the US as an over-the-counter demulcent.  Singers and voice-conscious communities use such teas for soothing. No clinical studies of these teas were found.

name: Honey and ginger throat soothing

angle.text: Users take honey and ginger in warm drinks to soothe the throat and keep the voice comfortable. Honey has some cough data and WHO guidance for sore throats, while ginger rests on traditional use; voice appearance is untested.

summary: Honey and ginger drinks for a sore throat; traditional, with some cough data for honey and little else.
note: No honey for infants under one.
currentQuick:
A kitchen remedy used for throat comfort.
Honey has some cough evidence; ginger's effectiveness for any disease is uncertain.
How it works: Proponents say honey coats and ginger soothes; mechanisms are not established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Infant botulism risk with honey; ginger can interact with anticoagulants. [1][2]
deepLead: Honey and ginger throat soothing is a folk remedy of taking honey, ginger or both in warm drinks for throat comfort. A Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found no strong evidence for or against honey for coughs, while the WHO recommends honey for coughs and sore throats.  Ginger has a long traditional medicine history, but its effectiveness for treating disease remains uncertain.

name: Vocal rest

angle.text: Users rest the voice after strain to recover a clear, steady sound. Vocal rest appears in vocal hygiene guidance for voice professionals and sits within research on vocal fatigue; its effect on voice appearance is untested.

summary: Resting the voice after strain; studied within the wider vocal-fatigue literature.
currentQuick:
Vocal rest means reducing talking or singing to let the voice recover.
It is part of standard vocal hygiene advice for voice professionals, and vocal fatigue has been studied in several small studies.
How it works: The premise is that less vocal loading lets fatigue and irritation settle. [4][7]
Risks and caveats: No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed; persistent voice problems are typically assessed by clinicians.
deepLead: Vocal rest is the practice of limiting or stopping speaking and singing to let the voice recover from strain. It is discussed in vocal hygiene guidance for voice professionals.  Research has examined vocal fatigue and recovery in singers and speakers.

name: Avoiding whispering

angle.text: Users speak softly instead of whispering to reduce strain and protect voice quality. The advice appears in voice-care discussion and rests on limited, indirect evidence.

summary: A voice-care habit of speaking softly instead of whispering; the claim rests on limited and indirect evidence.
note: Persistent hoarseness over two weeks is generally advised to be medically evaluated.
currentQuick:
Avoiding whispering means using quiet voiced speech rather than whispering when the voice is tired or hoarse. It is discussed as a vocal hygiene habit.
The claim that whispering strains the vocal cords is noted in reference works as applying to some people, and is sourced to a news article rather than a trial.
How it works: Whispering keeps the vocal folds apart and produces sound from air turbulence. Proponents say people often push harder to be heard, which may add strain; this mechanism was not tested in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Few risks are attached to the habit itself. Experts generally advise medical evaluation if hoarseness lasts more than two weeks.
deepLead:
Avoiding whispering is a voice-care habit in which a person speaks softly in a normal, voiced manner instead of whispering when trying to rest or protect the voice. It is discussed in appearance-related voice improvement as part of reducing vocal strain.
Phonetically, whispering is an unvoiced mode of speech in which the vocal folds are held apart and do not vibrate, while air turbulence between the arytenoid cartilages makes the sound. Wikipedia notes that whispering can strain the vocal cords more than regular speech for some people, who are advised to speak softly instead, but sources this to a 2011 newspaper article rather than a medical study.
Voice-therapy and vocal-hygiene literature summarised on Wikipedia lists reducing overall speech quantity, avoiding throat clearing and shouting, and staying hydrated, and does not specifically address whispering.

name: Treating acid reflux for voice

angle.text: Users manage laryngopharyngeal reflux to relieve hoarseness and improve voice quality. Treatment studies for LPR are mixed and the diagnosis is debated; effects on voice appearance specifically are untested.

summary: Reflux control as a route to a clearer voice; LPR treatment evidence is mixed and the diagnosis is debated.
note: Long-term PPI use and persistent hoarseness warrant clinician involvement.
currentQuick:
Some people with chronic hoarseness or throat clearing are evaluated for laryngopharyngeal reflux, and treat it to improve voice quality.
Trials of acid-suppressing drugs for LPR have shown mixed results, and diagnosis is described as difficult.
How it works: Reflux of stomach contents into the throat is thought to irritate the larynx, causing hoarseness and strain. Treatment combines diet and lifestyle changes, medication and sometimes surgery.
Risks and caveats: Hoarseness has many causes, and clinicians generally recommend evaluation when it persists. PPIs are prescription or over-the-counter drugs with their own adverse-effect profiles.
deepLead:
Treating acid reflux for voice refers to managing laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), sometimes called silent reflux, with the aim of relieving hoarseness and improving voice quality. LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the larynx, oropharynx or nasopharynx.
Hoarseness is considered a primary symptom of LPR and can lead to vocal strain and fatigue, and may progress to muscle tension dysphonia that can persist after reflux is controlled. Many patients have little or no heartburn.
Management commonly combines lifestyle measures, proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) and alginate products. Evidence for PPIs in LPR is described as mixed to disappointing, and the diagnosis itself is debated.

name: Quit smoking for voice

angle.text: Users quit smoking to avoid or reverse hoarseness and the lowered, rougher pitch linked to smoking. Smoking is a documented cause of vocal fold swelling, though studies focus on health rather than voice attractiveness.

summary: Stopping smoking to protect the voice; smoking is a documented cause of vocal fold swelling and hoarseness.
note: Existing vocal fold swelling may not reverse after quitting.
currentQuick:
Smoking is documented as a major cause of Reinke's edema, which lowers pitch and roughens the voice. Quitting is part of standard management.
Cessation is reported to stop progression but not necessarily undo existing swelling.
How it works: Smoke exposure causes fluid accumulation in the vocal fold cover, making the folds heavier and slower-vibrating.
Risks and caveats: Continued smoking raises the risk of precancerous changes and laryngeal cancer. Cessation support is available through clinicians.
deepLead:
Quitting smoking for voice refers to stopping tobacco use to avoid or reverse smoking-related voice changes such as hoarseness and a lowered, rougher pitch.
Smoking is described as the leading cause of Reinke's edema, a fluid buildup in the vocal folds that makes them vibrate more slowly, lowering pitch and causing hoarseness. Smoking is also linked to laryngeal cancer and listed as a cause of vocal fold injury.
Cessation is reported to halt progression of Reinke's edema but not to reverse existing swelling.

name: Whisky and cigar voice fad

chain: Smoking and drinking irritate vocal cords
angle.text: Some online circles promote smoking and drinking as a way to get a deep, husky voice that sounds attractive. The voice change itself is documented in some smokers, but as a sign of vocal cord disease; its attractiveness benefit rests on anecdote.

summary: Smoking and drinking for a husky voice; the voice change is real in some smokers but is documented as disease.
note: Smoking is linked to laryngeal cancer and vocal fold disease.
currentQuick:
Some people associate cigars, smoking and whisky with a deep husky voice. No source reviewed documents the fad's origin.
Medical sources describe smoking-related voice changes as results of Reinke's edema.
How it works: Smoke exposure is described as causing fluid buildup in the vocal folds, which lowers pitch and causes hoarseness.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include laryngeal cancer risk, precancerous changes, breathing difficulty from swelling and, in some cases, surgery.
deepLead:
The whisky and cigar voice fad refers to the idea, discussed in some online circles, that smoking and drinking produces a deep, husky voice that is attractive. The sources reviewed contain no material on its history or on community discussions of it.
Medical references do describe a real link between smoking and a lower, hoarse voice: smoking is the leading cause of Reinke's edema, which slows vocal fold vibration, lowers pitch and causes hoarseness. The same entry reports that smoking increases the risk of precancerous changes, and smoking is associated with laryngeal cancer.

name: Deep voice masculinity meta

angle.text: Looksmaxxing forums hold that a deeper voice signals masculinity and dominance and so raises perceived attractiveness and status. Voice physiology is well described, while the social-perception claim is discussed mostly through anecdote in these circles.

summary: The belief that a deeper voice signals dominance and masculinity; voice physiology is documented, the social claims were not examined here.
note: Sources reviewed did not cover perception research.
currentQuick:
The meta holds that lower pitch equals more masculine, dominant presence.
Sources reviewed document sex differences in voice pitch but not its social effects.
How it works: Pitch is set by vocal fold length, mass and tension; male folds are longer and thicker, giving lower pitch on average.
Risks and caveats: Attempts to deepen the voice by straining or irritants carry vocal health risks; the strain itself is described as a cause of injury.
deepLead:
The deep voice masculinity meta is the belief, found in looksmaxxing and related culture, that a lower voice pitch signals masculinity and dominance and so contributes to perceived attractiveness or status. The sources reviewed contain no community text or studies on these perceptions, so this article covers only the underlying voice facts.
Typical fundamental frequencies for adult speech are about 90 to 155 Hz for males and 165 to 255 Hz for females. Adult male vocal folds are longer and thicker than female folds, which usually produces a lower pitch, and a larger male vocal tract also lowers timbre.

name: Voice transformation software

angle.text: Voice changers alter pitch or timbre in real time or in post-processing, so a speaker can sound deeper or more resonant in calls, streams and recordings. The change is audible immediately; its use for appearance is mostly discussed informally and has not been studied.

summary: Software that shifts voice pitch or timbre, used for disguise, effects and content; no appearance-related evidence reviewed.
note: Effects apply only to the processed audio, not the user's actual voice.
currentQuick:
Voice transformation tools alter the pitch and tone of recorded or live speech.
Sources reviewed describe general uses like anonymity and music production.
How it works: Algorithms change the amplitude, pitch and tone of the audio signal, and cloning tools model a particular person's voice.
Risks and caveats: Voice cloning is associated in reference sources with social engineering concerns.
deepLead:
Voice transformation software changes the pitch or timbre of a speaker's voice, in real time or in post-processing. Wikipedia describes voice changers as hardware or software that alters pitch or timbre or adds distortion, with software versions now very common and using many algorithms. The sources reviewed contain no community discussion of its use for appearance or content creation.
Pitch alteration is described as key to changing a male voice to female or the reverse, and voice cloning software can mimic a specific person from recordings.

name: Podcast mic and EQ boost

angle.text: Users pair a close, directional microphone with a low-frequency EQ boost so recordings sound deeper, fuller and more resonant. The effect is audible straight away on recordings, though the speaker's own voice stays the same.

summary: Close-miking and low-end EQ make a recording sound deeper; the speaker's actual voice is unchanged.
note: Affects recordings only, not the live voice.
currentQuick:
This is audio processing aimed at making a recorded voice sound deeper. A directional microphone used close to the mouth naturally boosts bass, and EQ can add more.
No studies have examined it as an appearance or social-perception tool.
How it works: The proximity effect raises low frequencies when a speaker is near a directional microphone; EQ further adjusts frequency balance.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented. The effect exists only in the recording or broadcast.
deepLead:
A podcast microphone with an equalizer (EQ) boost is a recording setup in which a directional microphone is used close to the mouth and low frequencies are raised electronically, so that a recorded voice sounds deeper or fuller. It is discussed in voice-focused corners of appearance and self-improvement culture as a way to make a recorded voice sound more resonant.
Part of the effect is acoustic. Directional microphones such as cardioids boost bass when the sound source is very close, a phenomenon called the proximity effect, which makes voices sound warmer and fuller and which radio announcers are often said to use for an authoritative tone. Equalization is the separate, electronic adjustment of frequency balance. The change affects only the recording or broadcast, not the speaker's own voice.

name: Accent training

angle.text: People take accent coaching to be understood more easily or to sound closer to a target accent, which feeds into how polished they come across. Linguists note it takes sustained practice, and its effect on perceived appearance has not been studied.

summary: Coaching to change or clarify an accent; linguists say it takes years, and its appearance value is unstudied.
note: Full accent change can take years.
currentQuick:
Accent training teaches the sounds and rhythms of a target accent, usually to improve clarity.
It is offered by speech coaches and linguists; listener research exists but not on appearance outcomes.
How it works: Practice of target vowels, consonants, stress and intonation with feedback.
Risks and caveats: No physical harms documented; some linguists warn about unrealistic expectations.
deepLead:
Accent training, also called accent reduction or modification, is structured study of a language's sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation so speakers can be understood more easily or sound closer to a target accent. Speech-language pathologists, acting coaches and linguists offer it, and speech-language pathologists do not regard accents as disorders.
Some linguists caution that changing an accent takes years of interaction with native speakers. Research on listener adaptation finds that listeners tune to accents, with generalization depending on training conditions. A study of 1,699 listeners found that reactions to accents depended on communication context.

name: Speech pacing apps

angle.text: Users practice speaking speed and pauses with apps because listeners form impressions of confidence from pace. Pace and impressions are researched in general, while the apps themselves have not been tested for appearance outcomes.

summary: Apps for practicing speaking speed; pace affects impressions, but the apps themselves are untested.
note: No trials of pacing apps found.
currentQuick:
Pacing apps help people monitor and practice how fast and evenly they speak.
Speech-tempo research links perceived speed with perceived competence, but no studies test the apps.
How it works: Users record or speak while the app tracks pace, then adjust speed and pauses.
Risks and caveats: No harms documented.
deepLead:
Speech pacing apps are software tools that people use to practice the speed and pauses of their speaking. Pace is of interest in appearance and presence culture because listeners form impressions from it. Researchers distinguish speaking rate, which includes pauses, from articulation rate, which excludes them, and typical English speech runs at about four syllables per second, with a range of roughly 3.3 to 5.9 depending on context.
Linguist Howard Giles found that faster speakers of several English accents were rated as more competent, though judging tempo is described as open to subjective bias. No published trial has tested whether pacing apps change such impressions.

name: Public speaking course

chain: Repeated practice in front of audiences
angle.text: People take public speaking courses to build confidence and delivery, which they see as part of coming across as more commanding. Confidence gains are reported for such training, but little direct trial evidence addresses appearance-related outcomes.

summary: Structured speech training; linked to confidence, with little direct trial evidence on appearance-related outcomes.
currentQuick:
Courses and clubs teach people to deliver speeches and receive feedback.
Research associates such teaching with confidence, but evidence on anxiety reduction is limited.
How it works: Repeated practice with peer or instructor feedback.
Risks and caveats: No harms documented; cost and time only.
deepLead:
A public speaking course is structured training in delivering speeches to a live audience, offered by clubs, schools and commercial providers. It appears in self-improvement and presence-focused culture as a way to build confidence and delivery.
Public speaking has a long history in rhetoric, from Aristotle and Cicero onward, and fear of it (glossophobia) is often cited as a common phobia. Clubs such as Toastmasters International use peer evaluation and impromptu speaking practice. Studies cited on Wikipedia associate teaching public speaking with greater self-confidence, though direct research on anxiety reduction is limited.

name: Ear training

angle.text: Borrowed from music education, ear training is mentioned in voice discussions as a way to become aware of and control vocal pitch. It is well established for music skills, while its use for voice appearance is anecdotal and unstudied.

summary: Music pitch-recognition practice; borrowed for voice pitch awareness with no appearance studies.
currentQuick:
Ear training teaches musicians to identify pitches and intervals by listening.
Its use for voice presence is unstudied.
How it works: Repeated listening and identification exercises.
Risks and caveats: No harms documented.
deepLead:
Ear training is the practice of learning to recognize pitches, intervals, melodies, chords and rhythms by ear alone, a core part of formal music education. In looksmaxxing-adjacent voice discussions it is mentioned for pitch awareness, for example controlling vocal pitch.
Methods include solfege, interval and chord recognition, rhythm exercises and software or apps. One study reported that musical ear training was examined in cochlear implant users for speech and music perception. No studies have tested ear training for appearance or attractiveness outcomes.

name: Tongue stretching exercises

angle.text: Forum posters say tongue stretches lower the voice. The only trial found involves swallowing rehabilitation after stroke, so the voice-deepening idea rests on anecdote.

summary: Tongue stretches said to deepen the voice; the only trial is in stroke swallowing rehab, not voice.
note: Studied only for swallowing after stroke; no voice-pitch data.
currentQuick:
Tongue stretching exercises involve extending or stretching the tongue. Some voice-focused circles say they lower the voice.
The only trial located tested them in 25 stroke patients with swallowing difficulty, looking at tongue movement rather than voice.
How it works: In the clinical setting, a therapist stretches the tongue passively to improve its mobility. No mechanism linking this to lower vocal pitch has been tested.
Risks and caveats: No adverse effects were described in the available abstract, and no safety data exist for the voice-related use. No published study supports or refutes an effect on voice pitch.
deepLead:
Tongue stretching exercises are exercises in which the tongue is extended or held in a stretched position, either by the person alone or with assistance. In looksmaxxing and voice-related discussion they are sometimes said to lower the voice, although that purpose is not what the exercises have been studied for.
In the published literature, tongue stretching exercises appear in swallowing (dysphagia) rehabilitation. A small 2019 randomized controlled trial in 25 stroke patients with dysphagia tested a four-week program of dynamic and static passive tongue stretching delivered by an occupational therapist, and examined tongue motility and oromotor function. No published study located for this article has tested whether tongue stretching changes voice pitch in healthy people.

name: Gym and loud lifting for voice

angle.text: A folk belief in voice-focused corners of appearance culture holds that weight training, especially grunting or shouting while lifting, deepens the voice. No published study located has tested it.

summary: Folk belief that grunting while lifting deepens the voice; nothing has tested it.
note: Voice therapy sources list yelling as a behavior to avoid.
currentQuick:
This is a folk belief that lifting weights, especially while making loud sounds, lowers the voice.
No published study located has tested it, and the sources found are thin.
How it works: Believers point to strength training and testosterone or to loud vocalizing as practice. No tested mechanism exists.
Risks and caveats: Voice therapy guidance lists yelling and forceful phonation as phonotraumatic behaviors that hygiene approaches advise reducing.
deepLead:
"Gym and loud lifting for voice" refers to a folk belief that weight training, and in particular grunting or shouting while lifting, can deepen the voice. It circulates in voice-related corners of appearance culture, but no published study located for this article has tested it.
Reference sources describe adult speaking pitch as typically about 90 to 155 Hz in men and 165 to 255 Hz in women. Voice therapy, as practiced by speech-language pathologists, targets vocal fold closure, pitch, volume and quality, and its hygienic approach advises avoiding phonotraumatic behaviors such as yelling.
